review.detail: All seven linted hypotheses are correctly inherited through Theorem~\ref{thm:tikhonv_rate} and Proposition~\ref{prop:exist_lambda}, for both primal and exchanged problems. Expanding the score difference and applying the two moment equations gives $\mathbb E d_n=-\mathbb E[(\hat h-h_0)(X)(\hat q-q_0)(Z)]$. With $s=\min\{\beta_m,1\}$, the adjoint identity bounds this bias by $O_p(\delta_n^{(1+2s)/(1+s)})$; the stated rate condition makes its product with $\sqrt n$ vanish. Common-null-set boundedness and score continuity give the displayed conditional second-moment bound. The stipulated measurable version identifies both the conditional integrals and evaluation averages. Conditional Chebyshev, followed by averaging its bound truncated at one, makes the centered evaluation remainder $o_p(1)$. Finally, $\mathbb E\psi_0=0$ and the assumed positive finite variance give the classical central limit theorem. The repair preserves every conclusion and supplies the required evaluation coherence.

\begin{lemma}[Localized Concentration, \citep{foster2019orthogonal}]\label{lem:concentration}
For any $h\in \Hcal := \times_{i=1}^d \Hcal_i$ be a multi-valued outcome function, that is almost surely absolutely bounded by a constant. Let $\ell(Z; h(X))\in \R$ be a loss function that is $O(1)$-Lipschitz in $h(X)$, with respect to the $\ell_2$ norm. Let $\delta_n=\Omega\left(\sqrt{\frac{d\,\log\log(n) + \log(1/\zeta)}{n}}\right)$ be an upper bound on the critical radius of $\shull(\Hcal_i)$ for $i\in [d]$. Then for any fixed $h_*\in \Hcal$, w.p. $1-\zeta$: 
\begin{align}
    \forall h\in \Hcal: \left|(\E_n - \E)\left[\ell(Z; h(X)) - \ell(Z; h_0(X))\right]\right| = O\left(d\, \delta_n \sum_{i=1}^d \|h_i - h_{i,0}\|_{L_2} + d\,\delta_n^2\right)
\end{align}
%
If the loss is linear in $h(X)$, i.e. $\ell(Z; h(X) + h'(X)) = \ell(Z; h(X)) + \ell(Z; h'(X))$ and $\ell(Z;\alpha h(X)) = \alpha \ell(Z;h(X))$ for any scalar $\alpha$, then it suffices that we take $\delta_n=\Omega\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\zeta)}{n}}\right)$ that upper bounds the critical radius of $\shull(\Hcal_i)$ for $i\in [d]$.
\end{lemma}

\label{asp:closeness_deepiv}
The minimum-norm solution $h_0$ lies in $\mathcal H$.

ass:re-cd-realizability.says:
\label{asp:re_cd}
The conditional density $g_0$ belongs to $\mathcal G$, whose elements are conditional densities with respect to a common dominating measure.

ass:re-cd-density-bounds.says:

\[
g_0(x\mid z)\geqslant c_0, \qquad \sup_{g\in\mathcal G}\|g\|_\infty\leqslant C_G.
\]

\]
with probability at least $1-\xi$.

ass:cr-deepiv-density-radius.says: The $\beta$-independent sequence $\delta_{n,\mathcal G}=\delta_{n,\mathcal G}(\xi)$ upper-bounds the critical radius of $\mathcal G_0$

ass:cr-deepiv-hypothesis-radius.says:

\mathcal H

ass:mean-sq-continuity.says:
\label{asp:mean_sq_continuity}
 For all $ f\in \mathcal{F}$, $ \mathbb{E}\left[ m( W;f)^{2}\right] \leqslant O\left( \| f\| ^{2}\right)$.

ass:critical-radius-boundedness.says:
For a fixed $B<\infty$, suppose that $|m(W;f)|$, $|h(X)|$, and $|f(Z)|$ are a.s. bounded by $B$, uniformly over $ h\in \mathcal{H} ,f\in \mathcal{F}$. Suppose in addition that, for every integer $n\geqslant1$ and every $r>0$, the localized squared-loss suprema
\[
\sup_{\substack{h\in\mathcal H\\ \|h-h_0\|\leqslant r}}
\left|(\mathbb E_n-\mathbb E)[h(X)^2-h_0(X)^2]\right|
\quad\text{and}\quad
\sup_{\substack{h\in\mathcal H\\ \|h-h_0\|\leqslant r}}
\left|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\epsilon_i\{h(X_i)^2-h_0(X_i)^2\}\right|
\]
are measurable random variables under the fitting-sample law and its product with the independent Rademacher law, respectively. Regard the functions in $\mathcal H\cdotp\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal F$ as functions of $W$ through $(X,Z)$ and $Z$, respectively, and put
\[
\mathcal U=\operatorname{star}(m\circ\mathcal F)
\times\operatorname{star}(\mathcal H\cdotp\mathcal F)
\times\operatorname{star}(\mathcal F),
\qquad
\|u\|_{L_2(W;\mathbb R^3)}^2
=\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{j=1}^3u_j(W)^2\right].
\]
Define the loss with zero comparator by
\[
\operatorname{clip}_B(a)=\max\{-B,\min\{a,B\}\},
\qquad
\ell_B(u)=2u_1-2u_2-\operatorname{clip}_B(u_3)^2,
\qquad \ell_B(0)=0.
\]
Suppose also that, for every integer $n\geqslant1$ and every $r>0$, the localized loss suprema
\[
\sup_{\substack{u\in\mathcal U\\ \|u\|_{L_2(W;\mathbb R^3)}\leqslant r}}
\left|(\mathbb E_n-\mathbb E)[\ell_B(u(W))-\ell_B(0)]\right|
\quad\text{and}\quad
\sup_{\substack{u\in\mathcal U\\ \|u\|_{L_2(W;\mathbb R^3)}\leqslant r}}
\left|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\epsilon_i\{\ell_B(u(W_i))-\ell_B(0)\}\right|
\]
are measurable random variables under the fitting-sample law and its product with the independent Rademacher law, respectively. Whenever the primal and dual roles are exchanged, suppose that these same two localized loss suprema for the exchanged problem are measurable under its fitting-sample law and its product with the independent Rademacher law, respectively. For iterative TRAE, suppose in addition that the following fixed-population-center squared-loss processes are measurable. For every integer $n\geqslant1$, prescribed integer $t\geqslant1$, grid point $\lambda\in\Lambda_n\cap[\lambda_{\mathrm{IT}}^\circ,2]$ for which $\lambda_{\mathrm{IT}}^\circ$ is defined, radius $r>0$, and $j=1,\ldots,t$, put
\[
a_{j,\lambda}(h;X)
=\{h(X)-h_{j-1,\lambda}^*(X)\}^2
-\{h_{j,\lambda}^*(X)-h_{j-1,\lambda}^*(X)\}^2,
\qquad
d_{j,\lambda}(h;X)=\{h(X)-h_{j,\lambda}^*(X)\}^2,
\]
where the population iterates are defined by \eqref{eq:iter_population}. For each $v\in\{a_{j,\lambda},d_{j,\lambda}\}$, suppose that both
\[
\sup_{\substack{h\in\mathcal H\\\|h-h_{j,\lambda}^*\|\leqslant r}}
\left|(\mathbb E_n-\mathbb E)v(h;X)\right|
\quad\text{and}\quad
\sup_{\substack{h\in\mathcal H\\\|h-h_{j,\lambda}^*\|\leqslant r}}
\left|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\epsilon_i v(h;X_i)\right|
\]
are measurable under the fitting-sample law and its product with the independent Rademacher law, respectively, using the same function representatives as the empirical penalties. The zero-iterate comparison uses $\hat h_{0,\lambda}=h_{0,\lambda}^*=0$.

ass:normality-source-parameters.says:
\label{cor:normality}
Suppose that the assumptions of \cref{thm:tikhonv_rate} hold for both $h_0$ and $q_0$ with (potentially different) source conditions $\beta_h,\beta_q>0$.

ass:normality-confidence.says: Choose a deterministic sequence $\xi_n\downarrow0$, and run the primal and dual tuning rules at confidence levels $\xi_n/2$.

ass:normality-common-scale.says: Let a common deterministic sequence $\delta_n$ satisfy \eqref{eq:delta_trae} for both problems at these confidence levels.

ass:normality-rate.says:
Let $\beta_m=\max\{\beta_h,\beta_q\}$ and assume that $\delta_n$ satisfies
\[
\delta _{n} =o\left( n^{-\alpha _{\mathrm{dr}}}\right) ,\qquad
\alpha _{\mathrm{dr}} :=\frac{1+\min\{\beta _{m} ,1\}}{2+4\min\{\beta _{m} ,1\}} .
\]

ass:normality-independent-evaluation.says: Let $\hat h,\hat q$ be the adaptive adversarial Tikhonov estimators, trained and tuned independently of the evaluation sample used in $\hat\theta(\hat h,\hat q)$.

ass:rkhs-qp-spaces.says:
\label{prop:rkhs_qp}
Let $\mathcal H$ and $\mathcal F$ be the RKHSs generated by $k_{\mathcal H}$ and $k_{\mathcal F}$, and let $K_{\mathcal H}$, $K_{\mathcal F}$, and $P_\eta$ be defined as in \cref{sec:rkhs_computation}.

ass:rkhs-qp-representative.says: Among functions with the same fitting-sample evaluations, take the representative with minimum RKHS norm.

ass:common-dp-stability-domain.says: let $\mathcal S_n\subseteq(0,2]$ be a stability region.

ass:common-dp-stable-segment.says: Suppose that some grid point $\lambda^\circ$ satisfies $\Lambda_n\cap[\lambda^\circ,2]\subseteq\mathcal S_n$

ass:common-dp-monotonicity.says: that $A_n$ is nonincreasing over the grid points in $[\lambda^\circ,2]$

ass:calibration-valid-bounds.says: In the following analyses, $\delta_n$ and $\nu_n$ denote deterministic upper bounds multiplied by fixed constants large enough to absorb the concentration and stability constants.

ass:calibration-source-independence.says: These multipliers may depend on the boundedness, density-ratio, and mean-square-continuity constants, but are independent of $n$, $\lambda$, and the unknown source parameter.

ass:calibration-before-fitting.says: They are fixed before fitting the candidate estimators.

def:dp.says:
\label{def:dp} Given constants $\ell\in(1,\infty)$ and $\kappa\in(1,\infty)$, choose the regularization parameter $\lambda$ as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item If $ \| r_{\delta } \| \leqslant \kappa \delta $, choose $ h=0$, which corresponds to $ \lambda =\infty $.
    \item If $ \| r_{\delta } \|  >\kappa \delta $, choose $ \lambda $ such that 
    \[
\| \mathcal{T} h_{\lambda }^{\delta } -r_{\delta } \| \leqslant \kappa \delta \leqslant \| \mathcal{T} h_{\lambda '}^{\delta } -r_{\delta } \| ,
\]
    for some $ \lambda '\in [ \lambda ,\ell \lambda ]$.
\end{enumerate}

def:critical-radius.says:
For a function class $\mathcal F$, let $\operatorname{star}(\mathcal F)=\{\gamma f:\gamma\in[0,1],\ f\in\mathcal F\}$ and $\mathcal F-\mathcal F=\{f-f':f,f'\in\mathcal F\}$. For independent observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ from the input distribution, define the expected Rademacher complexity and its localized version by
\begin{align*}
\mathfrak R_n(\mathcal F)&=\mathbb E_{X_{1:n},\epsilon}\left[\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\left|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\epsilon_i f(X_i)\right|\right],\\
\mathfrak R_n(\delta;\mathcal F)&=\mathbb E_{X_{1:n},\epsilon}\left[\sup_{f\in\mathcal F,\,\|f\|\leqslant\delta}\left|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\epsilon_i f(X_i)\right|\right],
\end{align*}
where the $\epsilon_i$ are independent Rademacher variables, independent of the observations. The localized class uses the population norm. A deterministic critical radius $\delta_{n,\mathcal F}>0$ satisfies
\[
\delta_{n,\mathcal F}^2\geqslant \mathfrak R_n\bigl(\delta_{n,\mathcal F};\operatorname{star}(\mathcal F-\mathcal F)\bigr).
\]
For classes fitted on an independent preliminary sample, we apply this definition conditionally on that sample and use a common deterministic upper bound.

def:rdiv-estimator.says:
The RDIV fit is
\[
L_n(h)=\mathbb E_n[(Y-\hat{\mathcal T}h(Z))^2],
\qquad
\hat h_\lambda=\arg\min_{h\in\mathcal H}\{L_n(h)+\lambda\mathbb E_n[h(X)^2]\}.
\]

def:iter-trae-estimator.says:
The iterative TRAE uses the same population iterates \eqref{eq:iter_population} and initializes $\hat h_{0,\lambda}=0$. For $j=1,\ldots,t$, its empirical recursion is
\[
\hat h_{j,\lambda}=\arg\min_{h\in\mathcal H}\left\{L_n(h)+\lambda\|h-\hat h_{j-1,\lambda}\|_{2,n}^2\right\},
\]
where $L_n$ is the adversarial loss in \cref{sec:trae}.

def:dual-estimator.says:
For a test class $\mathcal S\subseteq\widetilde{\mathcal H}$, define the empirical loss
\[
L_{n}^{\text{dual}}( q) =\sup_{s\in\mathcal S}\mathbb{E}_{n}\left[ 2\tilde{m}( W;s) -2q(Z) s(X) -s( X)^{2}\right]
\]
and the adversarial Tikhonov regularization estimator,
\[
\hat{q} =\arg\min_{q\in \mathcal{Q}}\left\{ L_{n}^{\text{dual}}( q) +\lambda_{\mathrm{dp}}^{\text{dual}} \mathbb{E}_n[q(Z)^2]\right\} ,
\]
where we select $\lambda_{\mathrm{dp}}^{\text{dual}}$ with the discrepancy principle.

paper.title: Adaptive Estimation and Inference in Conditional Moment Models via the Discrepancy Principle
paper.html:
Abstract

We study adaptive estimation and inference in linear inverse problems defined by conditional moment restrictions. Regularization stabilizes such problems, but the regularization parameter depends on a source parameter that is almost never known. We develop a discrepancy principle that chooses this parameter from empirical losses and prescribed bounds on statistical error, without knowing the source parameter. The framework covers Regularized DeepIV (RDIV) and the Tikhonov Regularized Adversarial Estimator (TRAE). Under the stated realizability conditions and comparable fitting and calibration error bounds, both one-step procedures attain strong- and weak-error bounds that match known-source rates for source parameters up to one. We also extend the framework to iterative procedures under realizability of the population iterates, widening the range of source parameters covered by the rate comparison. Finally, we use these adaptive estimators to construct an asymptotically normal doubly robust estimator that adapts to the well-posedness of the primal and dual problems.

1 Introduction

Ill-posed inverse problems arise throughout causal inference and econometrics [Horowitz, 2014{b}], for example in nonparametric instrumental variable (IV) regression [Newey and Powell, 2003; Darolles et~al., 2011; Newey, 2013; Ai and Chen, 2003], proximal causal inference [Miao et~al., 2024{b}; Tchetgen~Tchetgen et~al., 2024], and missing-not-at-random problems [d’Haultfoeuille, 2010; Miao et~al., 2024{a}; Breunig and Haan, 2021; Li et~al., 2023]. We study estimating parameters defined by
θ0​=E[m~(W;h0​)],
where h↦m~(W;h) is a known linear map. The nuisance function h0​ solves the conditional moment problem
E[h0​(X)∣Z=z]=r0​(z),(1.1)
where X and Z are W-measurable random variables. The function r0​ represents the expectation of a known linear map: E[m(W;q)]=E[r0​(Z)q(Z)] for the test functions q that Section 2 introduces.
Two established approaches estimate nuisance functions from conditional moment restrictions. Linear inverse problem (LIP) methods formulate the restriction as an operator equation and regularize its solution [Carrasco et~al., 2007; Darolles et~al., 2011; Bennett et~al., 2023]. Sieve minimum distance methods approximate the unknown functions in finite-dimensional spaces and minimize a sample criterion [Ai and Chen, 2003; Chen and Pouzo, 2012]. We follow the LIP approach. Let ΠQ~​​ denote the mean-square projection onto a closed test space. The operator Th=ΠQ~​​E[h(X)∣Z=⋅] then turns (1.1) into the equation Th0​=r0​. We estimate the minimum-norm solution of this equation with regularized estimators over general hypothesis classes.
While many works use Tikhonov regularization for this inverse problem [Newey, 2013; Li et~al., 2024; Bennett et~al., 2026; Bennett et~al., 2023], a central challenge in applying LIP methods is selecting the regularization parameter. Known-smoothness rate analyses for the Tikhonov regularized adversarial estimator (TRAE) [Bennett et~al., 2026; Bennett et~al., 2023] and Regularized DeepIV (RDIV) [Li et~al., 2024] express the regularization level in terms of the source parameter—often encoded by the β-source condition (i.e., h0​=(T∗T)β/2w0​ for some w0​∈H~). Li et~al. (2024) also study model selection for RDIV. Our procedure selects the regularization level within a fixed hypothesis class. In practice, β is rarely known. A misspecified regularization parameter can lead to suboptimal convergence rates or even divergence. The L-curve offers a geometric criterion for choosing the regularization parameter from the solution and residual norms [Hansen, 1992]. Cross-validation (CV) is also widely used, but it requires repeatedly minimizing the loss and is computationally expensive. Moreover, CV typically selects the parameter that minimizes the weak metric; however, this method fails to directly imply a bound in the strong metric. This paper addresses this gap by introducing a discrepancy-principle framework for adaptively selecting a hyperparameter that does not require knowing the exact β.
We primarily use the discrepancy principle (DP) [Morozov, 1966] from classical inverse problems. DP adaptively selects the regularization parameter λ so that the empirical loss is on the same order as the estimated noise level. This data-driven process balances empirical fit and statistical noise. In particular, we extend the classical DP to address the following challenges in our setting. First, classical LIP assumes known operators; in our setting the conditional expectation operator T is unknown and must be estimated, either explicitly or implicitly, before solving the inverse problem. Second, classical DP assumes fixed, known noise in r0​, whereas our noise comes from empirical-process fluctuations and depends on the estimator; see, e.g., the localized concentration bounds in Foster and Syrgkanis (2023), Lemma~14. Third, classical DP is typically analyzed over full Hilbert spaces with closed-form regularized solutions, while we work with general hypothesis classes (e.g., neural networks) that satisfy inductive-bias assumptions.
In this paper, we propose a discrepancy-principle-based tuning rule without prior information about smoothness. Our main contributions are as follows.
  • We give a uniform discrepancy rule together with an oracle guarantee that apply to a large class of estimators, and we apply them to RDIV and TRAE. For source parameters up to one, and when fitting and calibration errors are comparable, we show that the discrepancy principle selects a regularization parameter with the same strong- and weak-error rates as in the known-source analysis.
  • We additionally extend the adaptive estimator to iterated regularized RDIV and TRAE, and we show that, for a prescribed iteration count t, the adaptive iterated estimator matches the known-source rates over the range β⩽2t−1.
  • We combine adaptive TRAE fits of the primal and dual problems into a doubly robust estimator of θ0​. We show that this estimator is asymptotically normal and can adapt to the well-posedness of either problem.
  • We evaluate the rule with kernel classes in two simulation designs, where the best fixed penalty changes by three orders of magnitude across settings. With a data-driven noise level, the selected penalty follows the best fixed penalty of each setting, and adaptive TRAE has smaller strong, weak, and target errors than any single fixed penalty.
The rest of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 sets up the problem, fixes notation, and reviews linear inverse problems and the discrepancy principle. Section 3 develops the adaptive regularization framework and proves the guarantees for RDIV, TRAE, and doubly robust estimation. Section 4 evaluates the rule in simulations with kernel classes, and the conclusion discusses implications and open directions.

1.1 Related Work

Nonparametric instrumental variables. Nonparametric IV estimation provides a central example of a statistical inverse problem. Sieve and kernel estimators address the ill-posedness of the conditional expectation operator through finite-dimensional approximation or regularization [Newey and Powell, 2003; Hall and Horowitz, 2005; Darolles et~al., 2011; Chen and Pouzo, 2012]. The resulting convergence rates depend on both the regularity of the structural function and the operator [Chen and Reiss, 2011; Florens et~al., 2011]. Recent estimators accommodate flexible function classes through kernel methods [Singh et~al., 2019; Muandet et~al., 2020], minimax formulations of the moment restrictions [Lewis and Syrgkanis, 2018; Dikkala et~al., 2020; Liao et~al., 2020; Bennett and Kallus, 2023], or two-stage learning of conditional expectations [Hartford et~al., 2017; Xu et~al., 2021; Li et~al., 2024]. Our analysis builds on the regularized least-squares estimator of Li et~al. (2024) and the regularized adversarial estimator of Bennett et~al. (2023).
Adaptive estimation in IV models. Data-driven regularization has an established literature in nonparametric IV models. Johannes and Schwarz (2011) develop a model-selection procedure that adapts over smoothness classes under restrictions on the conditional expectation operator. Horowitz (2014{a}) select the dimension of a series estimator through an empirical criterion and establish adaptation to unknown smoothness. Breunig and Johannes (2016) combine model selection and Lepski's method to estimate linear functionals at adaptive rates. More recently, Chen et~al. (2025) develop data-driven sieve dimension choices that attain optimal sup-norm rates for structural functions and their derivatives, together with adaptive uniform confidence bands. These procedures adapt the dimension of a sieve or series expansion. We instead fix a general hypothesis class and adapt the Tikhonov penalty itself, combining localized loss bounds for RDIV and TRAE [Li et~al., 2024; Bennett et~al., 2023] with a discrepancy search over a geometric grid.
Discrepancy principles and iterative regularization. The discrepancy principle chooses the amount of regularization by comparing an observed residual with a noise threshold [Morozov, 1966; Morozov, 1984]. Classical inverse-problem theory relates this rule to source conditions and explains how iterated Tikhonov regularization extends the range of smoothness that the estimator can use [Engl et~al., 1996; Nair et~al., 2003]. Statistical analyses account for the fluctuations of the residual itself. Blanchard et~al. (2018) establish oracle adaptation in the strong norm for residual stopping rules in linear inverse problems. Celisse and Wahl (2021) study discrepancy rules for kernel spectral estimators, including Tikhonov regularization, and derive oracle inequalities and adaptive rates for ordinary and smoothed residuals. Harrach et~al. (2020) analyze regularization with noise estimated from repeated measurements. Our conditional moment setting adds estimation of the operator and optimization over hypothesis classes. The projected RDIV discrepancy and the adversarial discrepancy account for these statistical errors within a common finite-grid selection argument. The iterative analyses apply this argument to a prescribed number of Tikhonov steps.
Inference on linear functionals. Inference on functionals of conditional moment solutions connects this regularization problem to semiparametric estimation [Ai and Chen, 2003]. Bennett et~al. (2026) characterize strongly identified linear functionals and construct debiased estimators from regularized primal and dual fits. Bennett et~al. (2023) develop source-condition double robustness, under which sufficiently favorable regularity of either inverse problem can support asymptotic normality, and analyze iterated adversarial Tikhonov estimators. We use their primal–dual representation and remainder analysis with discrepancy-selected nuisance estimators. This yields a sufficient condition for asymptotic normality expressed in the primal and dual source parameters while choosing the regularization levels from the data.

2 Preliminaries

Problem formulation. We observe independent copies of a random variable W and estimate a linear functional whose nuisance function is defined by a LIP. The target is
θ0​=E[m~(W;h0​)],
with a known linear functional h↦m~(W;h). Let X and Z be two W-measurable random variables, and let H~ and Q~​ be closed linear subspaces of L2​(X) and L2​(Z), respectively, where L2​(X) denotes square-integrable functions of X. Let H⊂H~ and Q⊂Q~​ be subsets of these function spaces. The classes H and Q may consist of bounded subsets of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, neural networks, or parametric families. We define the linear operator Th=ΠQ~​​E[h(X)∣Z=⋅], where ΠV​ denotes mean-square projection onto a closed subspace V. The nuisance function h0​ is defined as the minimum-norm solution in H~ to the LIP
Th0​=r0​,(2.1)
where r0​ is the Riesz representer of the continuous linear functional q↦E[m(W;q)], so that
E[m(W;q)]=E[r0​(Z)q(Z)],∀q∈Q~​.
We make the following assumption to ensure that solutions exist.
Assumption 2.1.
We have r0​∈R(T):={Th:h∈H~}.
Given an estimated solution h^ of (2.1), the strong and weak metrics are defined as
∥h^−h0​∥strong​=∥h^−h0​∥L2​​,∥h^−h0​∥weak​=∥T(h^−h0​)∥L2​​.
The weak metric measures error only after applying T, so ill-posedness lets a small weak error coexist with a large strong one. The adjoint of T is
T∗q=ΠH~​E[q(Z)∣X=⋅].
Let a0​ be the Riesz representer of h↦E[m~(W;h)], and let q0​ denote the minimum-norm solution, when it exists, of the dual inverse problem
T∗q0​=a0​.
When the dual problem has a solution, estimates of h0​ and q0​ yield the DR estimator [Bennett et~al., 2023] of θ0​,
θ^(h^,q^​)=En​[m~(W;h^)+m(W;q^​)−q^​(Z)h^(X)].
For Corollary 3.19, this empirical average is taken over an evaluation sample independent of the data used to fit and tune the nuisance estimators.
Linear inverse problems. Classical inverse-problem theory studies a noisy observation rδ​ of r0​, often with a known operator T and error bound ∥rδ​−r0​∥⩽δ. Inverting an ill-posed operator can amplify this perturbation. To illustrate this point, suppose that the operator T admits a countable singular value decomposition
Th=i=1∑∞​σi​⟨h,vi​⟩ui​,(2.2)
where σ1​⩾σ2​⩾⋯>0 are the positive singular values, and {vi​}i=1∞​ and {ui​}i=1∞​ form orthonormal bases of (kerT)⊥ and (kerT∗)⊥, respectively. The minimum-norm solution of (2.1) is
h0​=i=1∑∞​σi​⟨r0​,ui​⟩​vi​.
The inversion amplifies a perturbation along uk​ by 1/σk​. Tikhonov regularization controls this amplification by solving
hλδ​=arghmin​{∥Th−rδ​∥2+λ∥h∥2}.(2.3)
Larger values of λ shrink the solution toward zero; smaller values allow greater noise amplification. The discrepancy principle balances these effects through the residual.
Definition 2.2 (Discrepancy Principle).
Given constants ℓ∈(1,∞) and κ∈(1,∞), choose the regularization parameter λ as follows:
  1. If ∥rδ​∥⩽κδ, choose h=0, which corresponds to λ=∞.
  2. If ∥rδ​∥>κδ, choose λ such that
    ∥Thλδ​−rδ​∥⩽κδ⩽∥Thλ′δ​−rδ​∥,
    for some λ′∈[λ,ℓλ].
The first rule uses the default estimator h=0 when the observed right-hand side is no larger than the prescribed noise threshold. The second rule makes the residual ∥Thλδ​−rδ​∥ comparable to that threshold. This residual is measured after applying T; controlling the reconstruction error in the strong metric additionally requires regularity, such as a source condition. The safety factor κ>1 makes the second rule feasible: the true solution satisfies ∥Th0​−rδ​∥=∥r0​−rδ​∥⩽δ<κδ, so a residual at the threshold is attainable.
In our statistical setting, both T and r0​ are unknown, and this ignorance adds perturbations that the classical rule does not face. With an explicit operator estimate T^n​, the identity T^n​h0​=r0​+en​, where en​=(T^n​−T)h0​, exhibits one such perturbation. Calibration must also absorb empirical fluctuations and, for the raw RDIV squared loss, an irreducible outcome-noise floor. An adversarial estimator never forms T^n​ at all, reaching the operator instead through a minimax objective, so its discrepancy carries a different set of errors. One search rule covers both, with a statistical error threshold that may depend on λ.
To analyze Tikhonov regularization, we introduce the source condition, a standard assumption in the inverse-problem literature.
Assumption 2.3 (Source Condition).
Problem (2.1) satisfies the β-source condition for some β>0, i.e., there exists w0​∈H~ such that the minimum-norm solution of (2.1) satisfies h0​=(T∗T)β/2w0​.
If T is compact, then by (2.2), Assumption 2.3 implies that
i=1∑∞​σi2β​⟨h0​,vi​⟩2​<∞,
which quantifies the decay of the solution coefficients relative to the singular values. This assumption is standard [Morozov, 1966; Darolles et~al., 2011; Li et~al., 2024; Bennett et~al., 2026; Bennett et~al., 2023].
Notation. Throughout the paper, we use ∥⋅∥ for the L2​ norm with respect to the input distribution, i.e.,
∥h∥:=∥h∥L2​​=E[h(X)2]​, ∀h∈L2​(X)
and the L1​ norm ∥h∥1​=E[∣h(X)∣]. The same notation applies to functions of Z under their input distribution. Write ∥h∥2,n​={En​[h(X)2]}1/2 for the empirical norm. For real numbers, a∨b=max{a,b}, and log denotes the natural logarithm. We use En​[⋅] to denote an empirical average, with subscripts indicating the sample when several independent samples are used. We use the asymptotic-order notation o(⋅), O(⋅), Ω(⋅), and Θ(⋅); op​(1) denotes convergence to zero in probability. For a function class F, let star(F)={γf:γ∈[0,1], f∈F} and F−F={f−f′:f,f′∈F}. For independent observations X1​,…,Xn​ from the input distribution, define the expected Rademacher complexity and its localized version by
Rn​(F)Rn​(δ;F)​=EX1:n​,ϵ​[f∈Fsup​​n1​i=1∑n​ϵi​f(Xi​)​],=EX1:n​,ϵ​[f∈F,∥f∥⩽δsup​​n1​i=1∑n​ϵi​f(Xi​)​],​
where the ϵi​ are independent Rademacher variables, independent of the observations. The localized class uses the population norm. A deterministic critical radius δn,F​>0 satisfies
δn,F2​⩾Rn​(δn,F​;star(F−F)).
For classes fitted on an independent preliminary sample, we apply this definition conditionally on that sample and use a common deterministic upper bound.

3 Adaptive Regularization via the Discrepancy Principle

We now state a finite-grid oracle guarantee for the discrepancy rule applied to estimators of (2.1), and then check its conditions for two estimators: RDIV, which estimates the operator explicitly, and TRAE, which estimates the weak loss through an adversarial problem.

3.1 Discrepancy Principle for Conditional Moment Problems

Consider a family of candidate estimators {h^λ​:λ∈Λn​} and a nonnegative calibration statistic Dn​(h^λ​). Fix λ0​=2 and ρ∈[1/2,1), independent of n, and set
Kn​=⌈log(1/ρ)log(2n2)​⌉,Λn​={λk​=2ρk:k=0,…,Kn​}.
Then ∣Λn​∣=O(logn) and λKn​​⩽n−2. For a prescribed noise level An​(λ), we use the threshold 23​An​(λ). The rule computes the candidates from large to small regularization and returns the first point whose calibration statistic lies below this threshold.
If no candidate clears its threshold, the rule returns the terminal point λKn​​, so the selected estimator is defined for every outcome. Theorem 3.1 and Proposition 3.5, Proposition 3.13 show that the rule accepts a candidate, and so never reaches the fallback, on the events they describe.
When the rule accepts a noninitial parameter, the selected point λdp​ and its rejected predecessor λ′=λdp​/ρ∈[λdp​,2λdp​] satisfy
Dn​(h^λdp​​)⩽23​An​(λdp​),Dn​(h^λ′​)>23​An​(λ′).(3.1)
Acceptance at λdp​ bounds the weak error; rejection at λ′, or acceptance at an oracle point, keeps λdp​ from falling too far.
The statistic Dn​(h^λ​) plays the role of the squared residual in Definition 2.2, and 23​An​(λ) plays the role of κ2δ2. For RDIV, Dn​ is a squared residual computed from estimates of the operator and right-hand side. For TRAE, it is an empirical adversarial loss. The statistical bounds in (3.3) turn a small discrepancy into a small squared weak error. When the first accepted parameter has a predecessor, the two inequalities in (3.1) bracket the threshold at adjacent grid points with ratio 1/ρ∈(1,2].
The following theorem states conditions on the discrepancy bound and threshold under which the rule has an oracle guarantee. Throughout, ξ∈(0,1) is a generic confidence level; we absorb fixed numerical rescalings of ξ into the rate bounds and relabel it after intersecting finitely many event families.
Theorem 3.1 (Oracle guarantee for the discrepancy rule).
Let An​:Λn​→[0,∞), and let Sn​⊆(0,2] be a stability region. Fix constants CA​,CV​,Cb​>0 and exponents γ∈(0,1] and q>1, and write Bn​(λ)=Cb​λq. Suppose that, on an event En​ with probability at least 1−ξ, the discrepancy bound
Dn​(h^λ​)⩽An​(λ)+Bn​(λ),(3.2)
holds simultaneously over λ∈Λn​∩Sn​, and every λ∈Λn​∩Sn​ satisfies
∥T(h^λ​−h0​)∥2∥h^λ​−h0​∥2​⩽CA​{Dn​(h^λ​)+An​(λ)},⩽CV​[λDn​(h^λ​)+An​(λ)​+{Dn​(h^λ​)+An​(λ)}γ],​(3.3)
Suppose that some grid point λ∘ satisfies Λn​∩[λ∘,2]⊆Sn​, that An​ is nonincreasing over the grid points in [λ∘,2], and that
Bn​(λ∘)⩽21​An​(λ∘).(3.4)
Then 1 accepts a candidate before exhausting the grid, and returns a parameter satisfying λdp​⩾λ∘ with
∥T(h^λdp​​−h0​)∥2∥h^λdp​​−h0​∥2​⩽O{An​(λ∘)},⩽O{An​(λ∘)/λ∘+An​(λ∘)γ}.​(3.5)(10)​
The rule uses the statistical-error bound An​ without evaluating the unknown bias bound Bn​. It compares Dn​ with 23​An​. Condition (3.4) guarantees that such a point exists, so the rule accepts λ∘ whenever it reaches it; because the search runs from large to small regularization, it stops at some λdp​⩾λ∘. Acceptance at λdp​ caps the discrepancy there by 23​An​(λdp​), and monotonicity carries An​(λ) and An​(λ)/λ back to λ∘, which gives (3.5).
We will specify Dn​, An​, and Sn​ for RDIV and TRAE in the following subsections, writing Vn​ there for the method-specific component of An​(λ)/λ. The proof is in Appendix A.
Noise calibration. The tuning rule takes valid statistical-error bounds as inputs. In the following analyses, δn​ and νn​ denote deterministic upper bounds multiplied by fixed constants large enough to absorb the concentration and stability constants. These multipliers may depend on the boundedness, density-ratio, and mean-square-continuity constants, but are independent of n, λ, and the unknown source parameter. They are fixed before fitting the candidate estimators. The constants at​ and bt​ used for the iterative procedures also absorb the propagation constants for the prescribed iteration count. The discrepancy bounds in the Appendix show that such choices exist. This convention establishes adaptation to the source parameter conditional on valid bounds for the function classes and preliminary nuisances. Estimating all of these bounds from the data requires a separate calibration analysis.

3.2 Adaptive Regularized DeepIV Estimator

In the IV setting, r0​(z)=E[Y∣Z=z] and Th=E[h(X)∣Z=⋅]; thus, in this subsection, Q~​=L2​(Z) and T is the conditional expectation operator. The RDIV estimator first estimates the conditional density of X given Z with respect to a common dominating measure μ, then uses the resulting operator in a penalized least-squares problem [Li et~al., 2024]. For the analysis that follows, split the observations into three independent samples Ipre​,Ifit​,Ical​, each of size n. Fixed positive sample fractions give the same rates in the total sample size. On Ipre​, fit
g^​=argg∈Gmax​En,pre​[logg(X∣Z)],(T^h)(z)=∫h(x)g^​(x∣z)μ(dx),
and a regression estimate r^ of r0​ from Y on Z. Write En​=En,fit​ within this subsection. The RDIV fit is
Ln​(h)=En​[(Y−T^h(Z))2],h^λ​=argh∈Hmin​{Ln​(h)+λEn​[h(X)2]}.
We assume these empirical minima are attained and measurable.
The population squared loss decomposes into an outcome-noise level and the squared weak error:
σY∣Z2​:=E[(Y−r0​(Z))2],L(h):=E[(Y−Th(Z))2]=σY∣Z2​+∥T(h−h0​)∥2.
The raw loss exceeds the squared weak error by the constant σY∣Z2​, so it cannot be compared directly with a threshold for statistical error. We instead calibrate on Ical​ with the projected residual
Dn​(h)=En,cal​[(r^(Z)−T^h(Z))2].(3.7)
The preliminary sample makes r^ and T^ independent of Ical​. At their population values, with ground-truth r0​ and T, for a fixed h,
E[Dn​(h)]=∥r0​−Th∥2=∥T(h−h0​)∥2.
Calibration therefore requires one regression fit for r^ plus one loss evaluation per candidate, on top of the O(logn) regularized fits.
Assumption 3.2 (Solution realizability).
The minimum-norm solution h0​ lies in H.
Assumption 3.3 (Conditional-density realizability and nuisance rate).
The conditional density g0​ belongs to G, whose elements are conditional densities with respect to a common dominating measure. For fixed constants c0​,CG​>0,
g0​(x∣z)⩾c0​,g∈Gsup​∥g∥∞​⩽CG​.
For a prescribed β-independent accuracy bound δn,r​=δn,r​(ξ)⩾0, the nuisance satisfies
∥r^−r0​∥L2​(Z)​⩽δn,r​
with probability at least 1−ξ.
Assumption 3.4 (Boundedness and critical radius).
For a fixed B<∞, ∣Y∣⩽B almost surely, every h∈H satisfies ∣h(x)∣⩽B on the common support of the conditional densities, and ∣r^(z)∣⩽B. Clipping the nuisance to [−B,B] weakly decreases its L2​ error. For g∈G, write
(Tg​h)(z)=∫h(x)g(x∣z)μ(dx).

4 Experiments

The guarantees in Section 3 compare the selected estimator with a regularization level that depends on the unknown source parameter. A simulation can test this comparison only when the best regularization level changes from one problem to another. We therefore vary the instrument strength, the noise level, the sample size, and the shape of the structural function, and we compare the discrepancy rule with the best fixed penalty in each setting. We use kernel hypothesis and critic classes. For these classes each candidate h^λ​ is the exact penalized solution and has a closed form, so the comparison separates the choice of λ from optimization error. With neural networks, each candidate comes from a separate training run, and in our runs the empirical TRAE loss increased in about 30% of the steps from one grid point to the next smaller one. An exact penalized solution cannot behave this way. We leave the joint treatment of optimization error and tuning to future work.

4.1 Design

Linear Gaussian design. Let Z, V, and ε be independent standard normal variables, and set
X=ρZ+1−ρ2​V,Y=hs​(X)+aV+σε,
with a=0.5. The structural function is a Gaussian bump of width s, centered and scaled to unit variance under X∼N(0,1):
hs​(x)=ds​exp{−x2/(2s2)}−ms​​,ms​=s2+1​s​,ds2​=s2+2​s​−s2+1s2​.
The disturbance aV+σε is correlated with X and has mean zero given Z, so hs​ solves E[Y−h(X)∣Z]=0. In the basis of normalized Hermite polynomials, the conditional expectation operator is diagonal with singular values ρk, k⩾0. The operator is therefore injective, and a smaller ρ gives a more ill-posed problem. Appendix D shows that hs​ satisfies Assumption 2.3 if and only if
β<βmax​(s,ρ):=−2logρlog(1+s2)​.
Over the regimes below, βmax​ ranges from 0.46 at (s,ρ)=(0.7,0.65) to 17.2 at (s,ρ)=(2.2,0.95), so the source parameter lies on both sides of one.
Nonlinear design. The second design adds a binary treatment, a nonlinear first stage, and heteroskedastic noise. With Z, V, and ε as above, let A∣Z∼Bernoulli{expit(Z)} and
X=ρ{Z+0.6sin(1.5Z)}+0.5(A−21​)+1−ρ2​V,Y=g(X)+Aτ(X)+aV+σκ(Z)ε,
where g(x)=tanh(x)+0.8exp{−(x−0.5)2/0.5}, τ(x)=1+0.5sinx, and κ(z)2=0.5+expit(z). The hypothesis takes (A,X) and the instrument is (A,Z), so that h0​(a,x)=g(x)+aτ(x). Given A, the first stage is a Gaussian location family whose location is increasing in z with range R, so the operator is again injective.
Regimes. We cross ρ∈{0.65,0.8,0.95}, σ∈{0.1,1,3}, and n∈{500,1000,2000,4000,8000}. In the linear design, the share of Var(Y) due to noise grows from about 20% at σ=0.1 to about 90% at σ=3. For TRAE, the linear design also crosses s∈{0.7,2.2}, which gives 90 regimes; the comparison across the two designs uses s=0.7, so each design has 45 regimes. Each regime uses 50 data sets for TRAE and the first 20 of them for RDIV. The data sets are nested in n and share random numbers across the other factors, so all comparisons between methods and between regimes are paired.

4.2 Estimators and Noise Levels

Both estimators use the kernel k(u,u′)=1+exp(−∥u−u′∥2/2) for the hypothesis and, in TRAE, for the critic. The constant term allows functions that do not vanish at infinity, such as hs​ and its conditional mean. Outcomes are standardized on the fitting block. Each hypothesis is restricted to the eigenvectors of its Gram matrix whose eigenvalues exceed Nϵmach​​ times the largest one, where N is the size of the fitting block.
TRAE fits on the first half of the sample. Its critic is the RKHS of the same kernel with penalty η∥f∥2, η=10−3, which we profile out in closed form (Appendix D.1). RDIV splits the sample into four blocks of size n/4, used for the preliminary fits, the fit, calibration, and evaluation. On the preliminary block, a mixture density network estimates the conditional density of the continuous regressor given the instrument, and kernel ridge regression gives r^. Fifty draws per observation from the fitted density define T^. The second stage is then a kernel ridge problem, and Dn​ is the projected residual (3.7) on the calibration block.
The search uses the grid of 1 with λ0​=2 and search factor 1/2, so that λk​=21−k and the grid has between 16 and 26 points (4). On every data set we fit all grid points and λ=0 once. The discrepancy rule and every fixed penalty are evaluated on these same fits, so two methods that select the same λ return the same function.
Noise level. The theory takes An​ from prescribed bounds whose constants are unknown. We compare two choices. The fixed-scale rule uses (3.17) with constant one,
δN2​=Nloglog(eN)+log{(KN​+1)/ξ}​,ξ=0.1,
with An​=δN2​ for TRAE and An​(λ)=δN2​/λ+νN2​ for RDIV, where νN​ has the same form on the calibration block. The noise-floor rule sets An​(λ) to an estimate of the value the statistic would take if the residual of h^λ​ carried no information about Z. For TRAE, let e be the residual of h^λ​ on the fitting block. Multiplying the part the critic does not explain, (I−Pη​)e, by independent random signs removes any dependence on Z and keeps the scale of the residual. The expected discrepancy of the result is
An​(λ)=N1​i=1∑N​[Pη​]ii​[(I−Pη​)e]i2​.
For RDIV, An​(λ) adds the variance of T^h^λ​ on the calibration block, the variance of r^, and an estimate of ∥(T−T^)h^λ​∥2; Appendix D gives the formulas. Both noise-floor levels are bounded below by 1/N. We fixed the noise-floor rule as the primary rule on pilot data sets, before drawing the main ones. It is a data-driven choice of An​, and the theorems, which take An​ as prescribed, do not apply to it directly.
Comparison. For a method and a regime, let R be the mean squared error of the method over the data sets of the regime, and let R∗ be the smallest such value among the fixed grid penalties in this regime. We report the risk ratio R/R∗. A ratio of one means that the method does as well as the best penalty for this regime, chosen with knowledge of the truth. In practice a fixed penalty is set once and used for every problem. We therefore also report the best single fixed penalty, the grid value with the smallest geometric mean ratio over the regimes. It is chosen after all results are known, which favors the fixed approach.
We compute the strong error ∥h^−h0​∥2 and the weak error ∥T(h^−h0​)∥2 by quadrature, using the analytic structural function and operator. The target error is (θ^−θ0​)2, where θ0​=E[h0​(1,X)−h0​(0,X)] in the nonlinear design and θ0​=E[h0​(X+1)−h0​(X)] in the linear design. The estimate θ^ is the plug-in average over held-out observations.

4.3 Results

TRAE in the linear design. 1 summarizes the 90 regimes. Across them, the best fixed penalty for the strong error ranges from 2 to 2−9, and 1 shows that the selected penalty moves with it; the correlation between their logarithms is 0.90. No single penalty works in every regime. Each fixed grid value is more than 8 times worse than the best penalty in some regime, while the discrepancy rule is never more than 1.83 times worse. On the same data sets, the rule has lower strong error than the best single fixed penalty λ=2−4 in 58 of the 90 regimes. The paired difference exceeds two standard errors in 43 regimes in favor of the rule and in 12 against it. The rule also has lower risk than λ=0 in all 90 regimes. Its largest ratios occur at ρ=0.65 and n=500, where the best penalty sits at the top of the grid and the rule stops at a smaller one.
The fixed-scale rule is less accurate, with geometric mean ratios 1.24 for the strong error and 1.59 for the weak error. Its constant also matters: with constant 0.5 or 2 in place of one, the worst strong-error ratio becomes 14.8 or 8.2. The noise-floor rule has no such constant. At the threshold where the noise-floor rule stopped, the analytic h0​ would also have passed in 86% of the data sets. The search never reached the end of the grid and accepted the initial value λ0​=2 in 3% of the data sets. 2 shows the strong error against n for s=0.7. The adaptive curve stays close to the best fixed penalty of each regime, while each fixed penalty is accurate only for some (ρ,σ,n): λ=2−1 at small n and high noise, and λ=2−9 at large n and low noise.
Two designs, TRAE and RDIV. 2 adds the nonlinear design, RDIV, and the target error. TRAE improves on the best single fixed penalty in both designs and for all three errors. Its worst ratio is at most 2.19, compared with 4.72 to 13.43 for the best single fixed penalty. Its smallest margin is for the weak error in the nonlinear design, 1.31 against 1.41.
RDIV improves on the best single fixed penalty in the linear design for all three errors. In the nonlinear design it improves the target error, 1.22 against 1.40, is close on the strong error, 1.30 against 1.26, and is worse on the weak error, 1.64 against 1.23. Its search is also less stable at both ends of the sample-size range. In the linear design it accepted λ0​ in 53% of the data sets at n=500, and it reached the end of the grid in 7% of the data sets overall and in 17% to 20% at n=8000, mostly at the lowest noise level. Two features of RDIV may explain the difference. It fits and calibrates on different blocks with an estimated operator, so its statistic need not decrease along the grid. It increased by more than 5% in 18% of the grid steps, while the TRAE statistic never did. Its noise floor also depends on the estimated operator error.
Scope. We chose the regimes so that the best penalty changes across them, since this is the setting in which a tuning rule is needed. Within a single regime, the best fixed penalty for that regime is about as accurate as the rule, and usually more accurate. The Gaussian designs violate the boundedness conditions of our theorems, and the noise-floor rule uses a data-driven An​. The experiments therefore show how the rule behaves with exact penalized solutions under conditions that the theory does not cover.

5 Conclusion

We develop a discrepancy rule for choosing the regularization level in conditional moment models when the source smoothness is unknown. The rule sets its threshold from prescribed bounds on statistical error and applies to both RDIV and TRAE. Its oracle guarantee reduces the analysis of any such rule to two ingredients: a discrepancy bound and weak- and strong-error bounds, both holding at every grid point. This general principle applies to the noniterative and iterative versions of RDIV and TRAE, and it yields adaptive rates that match known-smoothness comparisons within the smoothness ranges stated in the theorems when the underlying statistical errors are comparable. The threshold still requires valid statistical-error bounds. In simulations with kernel classes, where every candidate is an exact penalized solution, the rule followed the best fixed penalty across settings in which that penalty changed by three orders of magnitude, and it stayed close to the best penalty of each setting. These results use a data-driven noise level. A calibration of the noise level that the theory covers, and the role of optimization error for neural network classes, remain open.

Since An,tT​(λ)⩾δn2​, δn2​⩾n−1, and n⩾NIT​(B), the terminal point is accepted. The first accepted index is therefore well defined; it is either zero or has a rejected predecessor in [λ,2λ]. Each grid candidate requires t minimax problems.

Proof of Theorem 3.18.
Write s=sn,tT​ and q=qt​. Boundedness gives the result directly when s>1, so consider s⩽1. The discrepancy bound (3.23) gives (3.2) with the bounds in (3.21). Lemma C.7 establishes (3.3) for every λ∈Sn​=[λIT∘​,2] with γ=β/(β+1). For all sufficiently large n, the point λIT∘​ defined in the main text exists and satisfies (3.4). Since λIT∘​⩾s​, on Sn​,
An,tT​(λ)=δn2​+λs​,Vn,tT​(λ)=λ2s​.
The noise level is therefore nonincreasing, and bt​⩾2 with λ⩽2 give An,tT​(λ)/λ⩽CVn,tT​(λ) on that segment. Apply Theorem 3.1 and (3.22). The weak bound follows directly, while the source-bias contribution to the strong bound satisfies
(sq/(q+1))β/(β+1)⩽s(q−1)/(q+1)
because q⩽β+1. This proves the two stated rates. Boundedness covers the remaining finitely many n, after we enlarge the fixed constants. Finally, 2t⩾β+1 gives q=β+1 and the displayed unsaturated rates.

Proof of Corollary 3.19.
Apply Theorem 3.14 to both nuisance estimators at the prescribed confidence levels ξn​/2. Their rate bounds then hold on a common event with probability at least 1−ξn​→1. Because βh​,βq​>0 and δn​→0, these bounds give
∥h^−h0​∥=op​(1),∥q^​−q0​∥=op​(1).(C.16)
The remaining bias condition is
n​E[(q^​(Z)−q0​(Z))(h^(X)−h0​(X))]=op​(1).(C.17)
Suppose first that βm​=βh​⩾βq​. By the adjoint identity and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,
​E[(q^​(Z)−q0​(Z))(h^(X)−h0​(X))]​​⩽∥h^−h0​∥∥T∗(q^​−q0​)∥=Op​(δnmin{βm​,1}/(1+min{βm​,1})​⋅δn​)=Op​(δn1+min{βm​,1}/(1+min{βm​,1})​).​

gives the same rate. By assumption, δn​=o(n−(1+min{βm​,1})/(2+4min{βm​,1})), and hence

which proves (C.17).
Original step For completeness, define the uncentered score
S(W;h,q)=m~(W;h)+m(W;q)−h(X)q(Z),dn​(W)=S(W;h^,q^​)−S(W;h0​,q0​).
Revised step Use the jointly measurable version of dn​ stipulated in Corollary 3.19. Its agreement with the fitted score difference for almost every training realization and almost every fresh observation identifies its conditional population integrals with those of the score difference. Its almost sure agreement at every evaluation observation identifies its evaluation average with the difference of the two evaluated score averages.
Conditional on the nuisance-training data, the evaluation observations are independent and identically distributed. Boundedness of the nuisance classes and the score continuity assumptions imply
E[dn​(W)2∣training]⩽C{∥h^−h0​∥γh​+∥q^​−q0​∥γq​+∥h^−h0​∥2+∥q^​−q0​∥2}=op​(1).
Conditional Chebyshev's inequality therefore gives n​(En,eval​−E)dn​=op​(1), where Edn​ integrates a fresh observation conditional on the training data. The primal and dual moment equations give
Edn​=−E[(h^(X)−h0​(X))(q^​(Z)−q0​(Z))].
Combining this identity with (C.17) yields
n​{θ^(h^,q^​)−θ0​}=n​1​i=1∑n​ψ0​(Wi​)+op​(1).
The moment equations also imply Eψ0​(W)=0. The classical central limit theorem applies because 0<E[ψ0​(W)2]<∞, proving the stated normal limit.

D Additional Experiment Details

Source condition in the linear design. Let ϕk​=Hek​/k!​ denote the normalized probabilists' Hermite polynomials, an orthonormal basis of L2​(N(0,1)). Since (X,Z) is a standard bivariate normal pair with correlation ρ, Mehler's formula gives E[ϕk​(X)∣Z]=ρkϕk​(Z), so T∗Tϕk​=ρ2kϕk​. The function hs​ is even and centered, so ⟨hs​,ϕ0​⟩=0 and ⟨hs​,ϕ2k+1​⟩=0. For k⩾1, a direct calculation gives
⟨hs​,ϕ2k​⟩=ds​ms​​2kk!(1+s2)k(−1)k(2k)!​​.
The source condition hs​=(T∗T)β/2w0​ holds if and only if
∥w0​∥2=k⩾1∑​ρ4kβ⟨hs​,ϕ2k​⟩2​=ds2​ms2​​k⩾1∑​(k2k​)4kqk​=ds2​ms2​​{(1−q)−1/2−1},q=(1+s2)2ρ−4β​,
is finite, that is, if and only if q<1. This is the condition β<βmax​(s,ρ) in Section 4.1. 3 gives its values.
Errors. Strong errors use a trapezoid rule on 2001 points in [−8,8] for the standard normal regressor. Weak errors integrate the analytic conditional law of X given the instrument over a grid in (Z,V) on [−6,6]2, with 241×161 points in the 90-regime study and 121×81 points in the two-design study. In the nonlinear design, both errors use a joint grid over (A,Z,V) weighted by P(A∣Z). The plug-in target uses the second half of the sample for TRAE and the last quarter for RDIV. In the nonlinear design, the continuous regressor is standardized with the mean and standard deviation of the first half of the sample.
RDIV nuisances and noise level. The mixture density network has 20 components and hidden width 64. It is trained by Adam with learning rate 10−3 and weight decay 10−4 for at most 300 epochs and stops after 25 epochs without improvement on a quarter of the preliminary block. The pilot r^ is kernel ridge regression on the preliminary block, with the kernel of Section 4.2 and ridge 10−3. Fifty draws per observation from the fitted density, frozen across candidates, define T^.
Let G and Gcal​ be the matrices that map the coordinates b of a hypothesis to T^h on the fitting and calibration blocks, and write G⊤G=Wdiag(μj​)W⊤. The candidate is b^λ​=(G⊤G+λI)−1G⊤y. Let σ^2 be the mean squared difference between y and r^(Z) on the fitting block. Treating the noise as homoskedastic with variance σ^2, the variance of T^h^λ​ on the calibration block is
σ^2j∑​(μj​+λ)2μj​​Ncal​∥Gcal​Wej​∥2​,
where ej​ is the jth unit vector. The pilot has the form r^(z)=w(z)⊤ypre​, and its variance term is ν^2=σ^2Ncal−1​∑i∈Ical​​∥w(Zi​)∥2. For the operator error, the difference h^λ​(Xi​)−T^h^λ​(Zi​) has conditional mean {(T−T^)h^λ​}(Zi​) given Zi​. On the calibration block, we evaluate the TRAE statistic with the kernel critic on Z at this difference, subtract its sign-flip level, and take the positive part. The noise level An​(λ) is the sum of the three terms.
Grids. 4 lists the fitting-block sizes and grid lengths. Every grid starts at λ0​=2 and halves at each step. The best fixed penalty of a regime is taken over its whole grid, and the best single fixed penalty over the grid values present at every sample size.
Pilot runs. Two pilot runs on seeds 1001–1008 fixed the noise-floor rule before the main seeds 2001–2050 were drawn. The first used 12 regimes of the linear design, with ρ∈{0.65,0.95}, s=0.7, σ∈{0.1,3}, and n∈{500,2000,8000}; the second used 16 regimes of both designs at n∈{1000,4000}. For RDIV, the operator-error term was added after the pilot showed that without it the search reached the end of the grid in up to 38% of the data sets. On the pilot, the fixed-scale RDIV level δN2​/λ+νN2​ performed about as well on the strong error and worse on the weak and target errors.
Provenance. The two studies are 20261001- gaussian- regimes (90 regimes, TRAE) and 20261001- regimes- v2 (two designs, TRAE and RDIV) in the project's experiment directory at source revision 5985a2c. Both contain every fitted candidate with its discrepancy, noise level, and errors, so all tables and figures can be rebuilt from them. In both studies the linear-design TRAE fits at s=0.7 coincide. The kernel computations ran on CPUs; the mixture density networks for RDIV ran on GPUs.

D.1 RKHS computation

Let N=n1​ be the fitting-sample size, y=(Y1​,…,YN​)⊤, and define the Gram matrices
[KH​]ij​=kH​(Xi​,Xj​),[KF​]ij​=kF​(Zi​,Zj​),Pη​=KF​(KF​+NηIN​)−1.
For the minimum-RKHS-norm representative hα​(x)=∑j=1N​αj​kH​(Xj​,x), the critic can be profiled out in closed form. Before the spectral restriction below, the RKHS TRAE fit at a positive candidate λ solves the convex quadratic program
αλ​∈argα∈RNmin​{(y−KH​α)⊤Pη​(y−KH​α)+λα⊤KH2​α}.(D.1)
Equivalently, after dropping the constant y⊤Pη​y, the objective is
α⊤(KH​Pη​KH​+λKH2​)α−2α⊤KH​Pη​y.
Both Pη​ and KH​ are positive semidefinite, so this objective is convex and its stationarity condition
(KH​Pη​KH​+λKH2​)α=KH​Pη​y(D.2)
identifies the minimizer. Proposition D.1 gives its minimum-Euclidean-norm solution, αλ​=(KH​Pη​KH​+λKH2​)†KH​Pη​y. Each candidate therefore costs a linear solve, with no iterative optimization.
A change of variable gives a well-conditioned computation on a prescribed spectral subspace. Let QH​ contain the orthonormal eigenvectors of KH​ whose eigenvalues exceed ϵH​λmax​(KH​), and let DH​ contain those eigenvalues. The default relative tolerance is ϵH​=Nϵmach​​. Restrict the hypothesis to the corresponding kernel span. Its fitting values have the form v=QH​a, and its coefficients are α=QH​DH−1​a. With
M=QH⊤​Pη​QH​,b=QH⊤​Pη​y,
the restricted quadratic program becomes
aλ​=argamin​{(y−QH​a)⊤Pη​(y−QH​a)+λ∥a∥2},(M+λI)aλ​=b.(D.3)
The matrix M is positive semidefinite with spectrum in [0,1), so the system has condition number at most (1+λ)/λ for λ>0.
Write M=Vdiag(mi​)V⊤ and t=V⊤b. Then the whole regularization path follows from
aλ​=Vdiag(mi​+λ1​)t,LN,η​(hλ​)=N1​(y−QH​aλ​)⊤Pη​(y−QH​aλ​).(D.4)
At λ=0, we use the minimum-Euclidean-norm solution after retaining compressed eigenvalues larger than the absolute numerical tolerance 10−12. The selection statistic and predictions use the same fitted function, since KH​αλ​=QH​aλ​ on the retained subspace. Kernel and compressed-matrix eigendecompositions are computed once; each subsequent candidate costs at most O(N2) operations. The computed fit minimizes the objective on the retained hypothesis span, up to numerical error. This restriction is an additional regularization choice and must be included in the experiment settings.
For RDIV, let y be the standardized outcomes on the fitting block, and restrict the hypothesis to the retained span as above, with coordinates b. Averaging the hypothesis features over the frozen draws from the fitted density gives a matrix G with Gb=(T^h(Zi​))i=1N​. The candidate minimizes N−1{∥y−Gb∥2+λ∥b∥2}, so that
(G⊤G+λI)bλ​=G⊤y,
and one eigendecomposition of G⊤G gives the whole path. The discrepancy is Ncal−1​∥r^cal​−Gcal​bλ​∥2, where Gcal​ is formed in the same way on the calibration block and r^cal​ contains the pilot values there. The retained span and the critic ridge are computational choices; the guarantees for bounded classes do not follow from these reductions alone.

D.2 RKHS reduction

For the kernel TRAE estimator in Section 4.2, define the ridge-stabilized empirical adversarial loss
LN,η​(h):=f∈Fsup​{N2​i=1∑N​{Yi​−h(Xi​)}f(Zi​)−N1​i=1∑N​f(Zi​)2−η∥f∥F2​},(D.5)
where F is the RKHS generated by kF​ and η>0. The fitted hypothesis minimizes
LN,η​(h)+Nλ​i=1∑N​h(Xi​)2.
Proposition D.1 (RKHS quadratic reduction).
Let H and F be the RKHSs generated by kH​ and kF​, and let KH​, KF​, and Pη​ be defined as in Appendix D.1. Among functions with the same fitting-sample evaluations, take the representative with minimum RKHS norm. Then the minimizer of
LN,η​(h)+λEN​[h(X)2]
has the form hλ​(⋅)=∑j=1N​αλ,j​kH​(Xj​,⋅), where αλ​ solves (D.1). The minimum-Euclidean-norm coefficient vector is
αλ​=(KH​Pη​KH​+λKH2​)†KH​Pη​y,(D.6)
where A† denotes the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of A.
Proof.
Fix h and write rh​=(Yi​−h(Xi​))i=1N​. The representer theorem gives a maximizing critic of the form
fγ​(⋅)=j=1∑N​γj​kF​(Zj​,⋅).
Its fitting-sample evaluations are KF​γ and its squared RKHS norm is γ⊤KF​γ. Substitution into (D.5) gives
γ∈RNsup​{N2​rh⊤​KF​γ−N1​γ⊤KF2​γ−ηγ⊤KF​γ}.
The first-order condition is
KF​{(KF​+NηIN​)γ−rh​}=0.
We may therefore take
γ​h​=(KF​+NηIN​)−1rh​.
Evaluating the objective at this coefficient vector yields
LN,η​(h)=N1​rh⊤​KF​(KF​+NηIN​)−1rh​=N1​rh⊤​Pη​rh​.(D.7)
The objective depends on h only through its fitting-sample evaluations. Its minimum-RKHS-norm representative consequently has the form hα​(⋅)=∑j=1N​αj​kH​(Xj​,⋅), with evaluation vector KH​α. Combining (D.7) with
EN​[hα​(X)2]=N1​α⊤KH2​α
and multiplying the objective by N gives (D.1). Since Pη​ is positive semidefinite, this is a convex quadratic program. Its first-order condition is
(KH​Pη​KH​+λKH2​)α=KH​Pη​y.
The Moore–Penrose solution in (D.6) is the minimum-Euclidean-norm solution of this system.
∎

comments.excerpt: \vsLine\textbf{Claim:} Assumption~\ref{asp:critical_radius} supplies bounded classes for the localized concentration arguments used in one-step and iterative TR
comments.label: PaperFormalizer
comments.html: Claim: Assumption 3.12 supplies bounded classes for the localized concentration arguments used in one-step and iterative TRAE. What is wrong: “For a fixed B<∞, suppose that ∣m(W;f)∣, ∣h(X)∣, and ∣f(Z)∣ are a.s. bounded by B, uniformly over h∈H,f∈F.” Uniform boundedness does not ensure measurability of the localized empirical and Rademacher loss suprema, and measurability for the h0​-centered squares and zero-comparator adversarial loss does not ensure it for squares centered at hj−1,λ∗​ or hj,λ∗​. Counterexample: Let A⊂(0,1/2) be non-Lebesgue-measurable, and let W=X=Z be uniform on [0,1] with completed Lebesgue law. Take H=L2​(X), Q​=span{1}, Th=E[h(X)], r0​=h0​=1, β=1, and w0​=1. Let F consist of the constant functions with values in [0,1], set m(W;f)=f, and take B=1. Using the supplied function representatives, take H={x↦c:0⩽c⩽1}∪{1−1{a}​:a∈[0,1]}∪{1−21​1{a}​:a∈A}. Take ρ=1/2 and t=2, use the measurable constant minimizers h^j,λ​=hj,λ∗​=1−{λ/(1+λ)}j, and choose sufficiently large deterministic calibrated critical-radius bounds of order {loglog(en)+log(t(Kn​+1)/ξ)+1}/n​. For sufficiently large n, the grid point λ=1 lies in the oracle segment, and the unshifted squared-loss and zero-comparator adversarial-loss suprema are measurable because the optional singleton increments are dominated by those indexed by all of [0,1]. Off the measurable null set of sample ties, suph∈H,∥h−1/2∥⩽1/2​∣(En​−E)(h(X)−1/2)2∣=(4n)−11{∃i:Xi​∈A}​ is not measurable, so the fixed-population-center concentration application lacks its required regularity. Proposed fix: Retain the boundedness, localized squared-loss, and zero-comparator adversarial-loss conditions, and add measurability of the displayed localized empirical and Rademacher suprema for aj,λ​ and dj,λ​ at every required fixed population center, using the same representatives as the penalties. All results assuming Assumption 3.12 inherit this condition, protecting Theorems 3.14 and 3.18 and Corollaries 3.19, C.3, and C.6 at full strength.

comments.excerpt: \vsLine\textbf{Claim:} Corollary~\ref{cor:normality} asserts asymptotic linearity and a normal limit for the independently evaluated doubly robust estimator. \v
comments.label: PaperFormalizer
comments.html:
Claim: Corollary 3.19 asserts asymptotic linearity and a normal limit for the independently evaluated doubly robust estimator. What is wrong: “For completeness, define the uncentered score
S(W;h,q)=m~(W;h)+m(W;q)−h(X)q(Z),dn​(W)=S(W;h^,q^​)−S(W;h0​,q0​).”
Defining the fitted score difference sectionwise does not ensure a jointly measurable version coherent with both its conditional population integrals and its evaluations on the finite evaluation sample. Counterexample: Let U and V be independent uniform random variables on [0,1], realized on the uncompleted Borel product probability space, with U representing training information and V a fresh observation. Let A⊂[0,1] be a non-Borel set. Consider the sectionwise representatives g(u,v)=1A​(u)1{0}​(v) and gˉ​(u,v)=0, which represent the same zero population-L2​ function for every fixed u. Every fixed-training section of g is measurable and has zero population-L2​ norm, but g(U,V) is not measurable on this product space because its nonzero set is A×{0}; choosing the coherent measurable version gˉ​ resolves this version ambiguity. Proposed fix: State explicitly the jointly measurable nuisance-evaluation versions and the coherent jointly measurable version of the fitted score difference, including agreement for almost every training realization and fresh observation and almost sure agreement throughout the finite evaluation sample; use that version in the proof, preserving the full asymptotic linearity and normal limit of Corollary 3.19.

comments.excerpt: \vsLine\textbf{Claim:} Lemma~\ref{lemma:t_err_dp} asserts the simultaneous density, nuisance, operator, and first-stage loss bounds with probability at least $1
comments.label: PaperFormalizer
comments.html: Claim: Lemma B.1 asserts the simultaneous density, nuisance, operator, and first-stage loss bounds with probability at least 1−ξ under Assumptions 3.3 and 3.4. What is wrong: (a) “… applied with g0​∈G and the critical radius of G0​, gives (B.1) with probability at least 1−ξ/2.” This step uses the conditional-MLE bound of Li et~al. (2024), Theorem~24, which the paper assumes only for the density lower bound and the conditions of the source's referenced RDIV theorem, including its source condition, but applies it to a model satisfying only Assumptions 3.3 and 3.4. (b) In the step quoted in (a): The cited theorem states an exponential confidence formula without a negative exponent, and its proof gives 1−exp(nδn2​), which is nonpositive and does not imply the asserted probability 1−ξ/2. Counterexample: Let μ be Lebesgue measure on [0,1], let Z be uniform on [0,1], and let ϕj​ be the mean-zero orthonormal Rademacher functions. Set σj​=2−j2−2 and g0​(x∣z)=1+∑j⩾1​σj​ϕj​(x)ϕj​(z); both marginals are uniform, and 1/2⩽g0​⩽2. Take H~=span​{1,ϕj​:j⩾1}⊆L2​(X) and Q~​=L2​(Z), so that Tϕj​=σj​ϕj​ and T∗Tϕj​=σj2​ϕj​. Set h0​=∑j⩾1​j−2ϕj​, r0​=Th0​, Y=r0​(Z), and r^=r0​. Take H={ch0​:1/2⩽c⩽3/2}, G={g0​,1}, B=3, c0​=1/2, and CG​=2. Choose δn,r​=0 and deterministic, β-independent critical-radius upper bounds satisfying the logarithmic floors in Assumption 3.4; these exist because the density class is finite and the primal and density-induced classes are bounded scalar intervals. Fix n⩾1 and ξ∈(0,1). These objects satisfy Assumptions 3.3 and 3.4, but ∑j⩾1​j−4σj−2β​=∞ for every β>0, so the cited source condition fails; moreover, 1−exp(nδn,G2​)⩽0<1−ξ/2, so the reported confidence formula supplies no asserted positive probability guarantee even in this model. Proposed fix: Replace the invocation of Theorem 24 by an explicit density-only specialization of the source's Localized Concentration lemma to the centered likelihood-transform class, followed by empirical likelihood optimality and a direct Hellinger comparison. This changes only the proof, adds no source condition, and protects Theorems 3.6 and 3.9 and Corollaries B.5 and B.9 at full strength.
